extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematical researchers (including advanced students and problem setters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, formulating, and judging mathematical problems and their solutions — what makes a good problem, what a perfect solution must satisfy, and methodological rules for developing methods and axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and ease of comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical problem should be clear and easily comprehended; clearness and ease of comprehension attract, while the complicated repels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasizes that a theory (and even more so a problem) be so clear that it can be explained simply; clarity makes a problem attractive and accessible to workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate difficulty (enticing but accessible)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical problem should be difficult in order to entice us, yet not completely inaccessible, lest it mock at our efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The problem ought to be a 'guide post' — challenging enough to provoke new methods and pleasure in solution, but solvable (or resolvable as impossible) so effort is not wasted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific significance / usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should have deep significance for the advance of mathematical science and play an important role in the investigator's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert gives historical examples (Bernoulli's brachistochrone, Fermat's problem, the three-body problem) showing that apparently special problems can lead to major new theories and methods across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor: correctness established by a finite number of steps from explicitly stated hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution shall be possible to establish by means of a finite number of steps based upon a finite number of hypotheses which are implied in the statement of the problem and which must always be exactly formulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the requirement of logical deduction; rigor is essential and corresponds to a universal philosophical necessity. Hilbert opposes informal or indefinite reasoning in solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact formulation of hypotheses and axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses must always be exactly formulated; axioms should give an exact and complete description of relations among elementary ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any statement is held correct only if derivable from the axioms by a finite number of logical steps. This includes describing new concepts by simple and complete systems of axioms so their exactness and deductive applicability equal classical arithmetical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor promotes simplicity and further development
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor in proof is not the enemy of simplicity; rather, the effort for rigor forces the discovery of simpler, more developable methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert cites examples (algebraic curves, power series, calculus of variations) where rigorous methods led to simplification and new advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic investigation of symbols and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: New concepts correspond to new signs; the use of geometric or arithmetical signs as means of strict proof presupposes exact knowledge and complete mastery of the axioms underlying those figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphic and mnemonic symbols (figures, diagrams, algebraic notation) are indispensable, but must be incorporated into the mathematical treasure only after rigorous axiomatic investigation of their conceptual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include geometric/mechanical/physical concepts in rigorous axiomatization (avoid one-sided rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat only analysis or arithmetic as amenable to rigorous treatment; geometry, mechanics, and physics concepts should be investigated and established on a simple, complete system of axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert argues that excluding these areas from rigorous treatment would cut vital branches from mathematics; instead, their ideas should be axiomatized so exactness matches arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek the more general standpoint to obtain general methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures often come from not recognizing the more general standpoint from which the present problem is a single link in a chain; finding that standpoint yields methods applicable to related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cauchy's complex integration and Kummer's introduction of ideals. The approach of finding a broader perspective is 'the most practicable and the most certain' route to methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and solving simpler subproblems first
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialization often plays an even more important role than generalization: solve simpler and easier related problems (possibly incompletely solved) to build up concepts and devices capable of generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert calls this one of the most important levers for overcoming difficulties; it is frequently used consciously or unconsciously by mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove impossibility when solution under given hypotheses is unattainable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the solution cannot be attained under given hypotheses or in the contemplated sense, one must show the impossibility of a solution under those hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impossibility proofs are valuable outcomes (ancients' irrationality proofs, squaring the circle alternatives); showing impossibility can settle a definite mathematical problem as fully as exhibiting a solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conviction of solvability (no ignorabimus) — target: finite logical settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is the conviction (axiom) that every definite mathematical problem must be susceptible of an exact settlement, either by an actual answer or by a proof of impossibility, via a finite number of logical processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This belief is a powerful incentive; Hilbert contrasts mathematical resolvability with persistent 'ignorabimus' and cites that even apparently unapproachable problems should be answerable by finite logical means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility (consistency) and independence of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: When testing foundations, set up axioms that are exact and complete, then ask whether certain statements (or axioms) depend on others and, above all, prove that the axioms are not contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert recommends proving non-contradiction (consistency) of arithmetic and geometric axioms (e.g., by constructing models or finding direct proofs), and isolating independent parts to achieve an independent axiom system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical existence via proof of non-contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: If contradictory attributes are never derivable from axioms by finite logical processes, then the mathematical existence of the concept (e.g., continuum or system of real numbers) is thereby proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert frames existence as consistency: proving compatibility of axioms proves existence of the complete system they describe; conversely, systems that cannot be axiomatized consistently are 'mathematically non-existent' in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize unnecessary postulates; seek transformations to reduce assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a theory assumes extra conditions (e.g., differentiability in Lie's theory of continuous groups), ask whether those assumptions are unavoidable or whether transformations/introductions of variables can reduce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert urges investigation of whether Lie's differentiability assumption can be dispensed with or derived from group concept and geometric axioms, and whether groups can be transformed into analytic groups under mild assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems as sources of methods and cross-fertilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular difficult problems can spur the invention of new methods and discoveries that impact many branches (a special problem may find applications in unlike fields).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes many historical cases (shortest line problem influences geometry, mechanics, calculus of variations; Klein's icosahedron links geometry, group theory, equations), recommending problems that encourage broad method development.
